storyboard.claim: An inferiority complex is using a subjective feeling of inferiority as a permanent structural excuse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher laying out Adler's definition in the study — no icon reads literally as an excuse, so the speaker and the phrase carry it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives Adler's definition of the inferiority complex the previous beat said he would define.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the frame adds only the speaker and the phrase; the definition itself is the audio.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher holds up a hand mid-explanation: the feeling is being built into an excuse.

storyboard.claim: You harden the worldview settled in childhood into a titanium shield you hide behind.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A shield — the defensive armor the narration names literally.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the definition of the complex to what it does for you: it protects.
storyboard.addedInformation: Makes the defense literal — a shield held up instead of an argument offered.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher raises a shield: an old childhood worldview hardened into armor.

storyboard.claim: The youth interrupts to test the theory with a hard case: no degree, real rejection.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man leaning in, finger up, raising his counter-example.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Cuts from the philosopher's definition to the objection it provokes.
storyboard.addedInformation: Signals the interruption is an adversarial test of the claim, not agreement.
storyboard.staging: The young man leans forward, hand raised: he is playing devil's advocate.

storyboard.claim: The rejection was a cold hard societal fact — an objective block, not a subjective interpretation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man facing a closed door, holding the rejection letter that names the missing degree.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Supplies the concrete evidence behind the devil's-advocate case just raised.
storyboard.addedInformation: The shut door shows the block is external and dated — a letter in his hand, not a feeling.
storyboard.staging: The young man holds a rejection letter at a closed door: society turned him away.

storyboard.claim: The objection — structural inequality is real — is a valid push back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man pressing the objection home, still holding the floor.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the objection as legitimate instead of brushing it aside.
storyboard.addedInformation: The concession is visible: the challenger keeps the floor rather than being talked over.
storyboard.staging: The young man points mid-argument: his push back lands and is accepted.

storyboard.claim: Adler does not deny that tangible obstacles exist; he separates meeting one from adopting a permanent excuse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A boulder sitting in the path — the tangible obstacle Adler concedes is real.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the valid objection by granting its premise: the barriers are real.
storyboard.addedInformation: The boulder makes the concession concrete — Adler's claim is not that obstacles are imaginary.
storyboard.staging: Adler gestures at the boulder in the path: yes, the obstacle is there.

storyboard.claim: The missing degree blocks one job on one particular day — a situational fact.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher conceding the narrow, dated consequence with a measured shrug.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Narrows the boulder down to the single case the youth described.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks the barrier as bounded in scope and time — not a lifelong condition.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher counts the point off on one finger: only that job, only that Tuesday.

storyboard.claim: Internalizing the block turns a situational obstacle into an identity-level excuse.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A mirror — the obstacle now written onto who he is instead of what happened to him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the situational barrier to the story he tells about himself.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mirror shows the obstacle moved inside and became self-image.
storyboard.staging: The young man frowns at his reflection: I am uneducated becomes who he is.

storyboard.claim: The cause-and-effect story is used to justify giving up on your own growth — and the complex then mutates into its opposite.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler naming the mechanism, one hand sweeping toward the reversal it sets up.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the purpose of the identity excuse just shown: it exists in order to stop.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names the teleological move — the excuse is chosen for the quitting it permits.
storyboard.staging: Adler points outward: the apparent cause and effect licenses giving up.

storyboard.claim: The opposite pole is a superiority complex — not simply arrogant people acting tough.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A trophy — the inflated status the complex performs rather than earns.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the opposite the previous beat just announced.
storyboard.addedInformation: The trophy shows the complex is about performed rank, not strength.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher holds up a trophy he has not won: the superiority complex on display.

storyboard.claim: Unable to tolerate the pain of inferiority and lacking the courage for real effort, people take an easy way out.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-step flow: psychological pain -> easy way out.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains how the inferiority feeling produces the superiority performance.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows cause and effect as one chain out of a single long sentence.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher traces the chain in the air as the two steps appear.

storyboard.claim: They want the status without the work — bragging about past glories and wearing expensive brands to inflate importance.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A mask — importance worn over an empty track record.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Gives the first example of the easy way out.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mask says the status is worn, not earned.
storyboard.staging: The young man boasts with a hollow swagger: the pride is a costume.

storyboard.claim: The subtlest form of the superiority complex is boasting about one's own misfortune.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man advertising his wounds outward while a sad face stays fixed — suffering sold as status.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Escalates from bragging about glories to bragging about pain.
storyboard.addedInformation: The sad face over a boasting posture shows the misery is being performed, not shared.
storyboard.staging: The young man lifts his chin and broadcasts his grievance: misfortune worn as a badge.

storyboard.claim: Trauma, difficult upbringing and physical ailments become a weapon of superiority.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sword — the wound swung at other people.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the function of the misfortune just shown.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns the passive victim into an aggressor: the pain is wielded.
storyboard.staging: The young man brandishes his suffering like a blade: it puts everyone else below him.

storyboard.claim: The claim is that this pain is entirely unique, profoundly deep and incomprehensible to anyone else.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man alone at the center, others held outside a circle he says they cannot enter.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the belief that makes the weapon work.
storyboard.addedInformation: The isolation is staged as a wall of specialness, not a plea for help.
storyboard.staging: The young man holds others at arm's length: nobody could understand this pain.

storyboard.claim: On the pedestal they become the special, untouchable center of attention.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A ladder beside the elevated young man while every face in the room turns to him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The payoff of the unique-pain claim: position above others.
storyboard.addedInformation: The ladder shows the superiority is a climbed position, not a fact about him.
storyboard.staging: The young man preens above the onlookers: he has made himself the center.

storyboard.claim: Woundedness is used to control the people around them, forcing others to walk on eggshells.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A puppeteer's cross above the others — one hand on everyone's strings.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the position on the pedestal to what that position is used for.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strings make the manipulation literal: everyone else moves carefully now.
storyboard.staging: The young man works the strings while others freeze mid-step.

storyboard.claim: Using your circumstances as an excuse means carrying the world's supposed judgments as if they were objective truths.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Chains of other people's verdicts draped over the speaker's shoulders.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Ties the superiority tricks back to the book's engine of borrowed judgments.
storyboard.addedInformation: The chains show the judgments are carried and never handed back.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher hauls a chain of other people's verdicts across his shoulders.

storyboard.claim: The question to ask is whose task the validation is — and it is yours, not society's.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher turning the book's core question on the youth, palm open.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Reframes the borrowed judgments as a task that belongs to someone.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the separation-of-tasks test the rest of the book applies.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher holds the question out: whose job is validating you?

storyboard.claim: That fear of real engagement leads into the most sweeping claim in the entire book.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher pausing before the big statement while the youth braces for it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Signals the turn from personal neurosis to our place in the universe.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the picture only marks the gear-change; the claim itself arrives in the audio.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher lifts a finger before the sentence: the biggest claim is coming.

storyboard.claim: The listener is asked to imagine floating completely alone in the dark silent void of the universe.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The philosopher opens the thought experiment as a dark empty field spreads behind them.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Begins the visualization the sweeping claim needs.
storyboard.addedInformation: Establishes the void stage that the next beats strip bare.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher gestures into the darkness: picture yourself alone out there.

storyboard.claim: The void is total emptiness — no language, no logic, no one to hear you, no stars, no planets, no history.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A lone silhouetted figure in pure black — deliberately no stars or planets, because the narration denies them.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Strips the void of everything, item by item.
storyboard.addedInformation: Honest negation: showing nothing instead of drawing the stars the narrator says are absent.
storyboard.staging: The young man hangs alone in blackness, arms drawn in: nothing exists around him.

storyboard.claim: Truly existing in that state would make every problem you currently have evaporate instantly.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same black void — there is nothing left in it to hold a problem.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the consequence of the emptiness just established.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the void adds only absence; the verb does all the work.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher speaks into the emptiness: a problem cannot survive this much nothing.

storyboard.claim: All problems are interpersonal relationship problems: take other people away and the very concept of a problem vanishes.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-step flow: take people away -> problem vanishes.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the rule behind the void's problem-free state.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the removal and the disappearance as one causal chain.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher makes a sweeping gesture: remove everyone and the problem goes too.

storyboard.claim: The obvious objection: floating in a void, surely you would be lonely.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man raising the objection from inside the void, hand to his chin.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Challenges the void claim with the first human counter-example.
storyboard.addedInformation: Voices the doubt the viewer is likely having at exactly this moment.
storyboard.staging: The young man frowns in the dark: alone must mean lonely.

storyboard.claim: Loneliness is not being objectively alone — it is being excluded from a community that exists around you.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A closed door with the young man outside it and a group gathered on the far side.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the loneliness objection by relocating it among other people.
storyboard.addedInformation: The door shows exclusion needs both sides — someone inside has to shut you out.
storyboard.staging: The young man stands shut out while voices gather behind the closed door.

storyboard.claim: Shame and late-night self-hatred are arguments in your head with someone who is not in the room — a standard set by other people.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A law tablet — the rule other people wrote — beside a youth arguing with an empty chair.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows where the excluded person's real interlocutor lives: inside his own head.
storyboard.addedInformation: The empty chair makes someone who is not in the room literal; the law icon names whose rule is being enforced.
storyboard.staging: The young man argues late at night with an empty chair: the judge already left.

storyboard.claim: The youth breaks through to why he actively chose to dislike himself.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A lightbulb over the cornered youth as the realization lands painfully.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the hidden argument to the moment he finally sees it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks this as the emotional pivot of the dialogue, not one more point in the debate.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher stands over the stricken youth as the lightbulb lands: he chose this.

storyboard.claim: He is terrified of being judged and of the pain of interpersonal relationships.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man folding in on himself, backing away from any contact.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the fear behind the self-dislike just uncovered.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns the abstract breakthrough into a bodily flinch a mute viewer can read.
storyboard.staging: The young man curls inward, arms tight: relationships are the thing he dreads.

storyboard.claim: He actively chose to hate himself, hyperfocusing on his own flaws — pimples, awkwardness.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A mirror — the flaws chosen into close focus rather than discovered.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The content of the breakthrough: the dislike was chosen, not assigned.
storyboard.addedInformation: The mirror makes hyperfocusing an action he performs, not a fact he uncovers.
storyboard.staging: The young man leans into the mirror, hunting pimples and awkwardness.

storyboard.claim: Self-dislike keeps him safely in his shell and pre-writes his justification when people reject him.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A shield — protection that doubles as the ready-made excuse for every rejection.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains what the chosen self-hatred buys him.
storyboard.addedInformation: The shield shows safety first, so the excuse that follows reads as its dividend.
storyboard.staging: The young man shrinks behind the shield, already rehearsing: of course they rejected me.

storyboard.claim: Self-hatred is a preemptive strike against the unpredictable pain of interpersonal rejection.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man jabs a finger at his own chest — the first blow aimed at himself before anyone moves.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the defense mechanism the shell just demonstrated.
storyboard.addedInformation: The staging shows the direction of the attack: himself, first, on purpose.
storyboard.staging: The young man strikes before anyone can speak: he rejects himself first.

storyboard.claim: The youth pushes back: some things lie outside human control, so not every problem is interpersonal.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man holding up a hand to stop the theory mid-flow.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Turns the armor argument into the objection it cannot yet answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks the boundary the next beats must defend — mortality, illness, dread.
storyboard.staging: The young man cuts in: what about what nobody controls?

storyboard.claim: The hard case: sitting alone in a room, contemplating the biological fact of dying one day.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An hourglass — his own time running out while he sits alone with it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: States the first concrete case outside human control.
storyboard.addedInformation: The hourglass turns mortality into a countdown instead of an abstraction.
storyboard.staging: The young man sits alone watching the sand: one day he dies.

callout.text: is this just an interpersonal problem?

storyboard.claim: And a person suffering alone from a terminal illness — is even that only an interpersonal problem?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man presses the hardest case directly at the philosopher: a life ending alone.
storyboard.onScreenText: is this just an interpersonal problem?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Adds the second hard case: suffering in a body, alone.
storyboard.addedInformation: Grounds the abstraction in a real patient, so the challenge is about dying, not a thought experiment.
storyboard.staging: The young man presses the question: is dying alone a people problem?

storyboard.claim: The youth argues that human beings have loftier philosophical problems than getting along with co-workers.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The young man raising the objection straight to the philosopher's face.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalizes the two hard cases into one philosophical challenge.
storyboard.addedInformation: Names what is at stake — dignity above mere social comfort.
storyboard.staging: The young man lifts his chin: philosophy is bigger than coworker harmony.

storyboard.claim: Adler's response: there is no such thing as a worry completely defined by the individual in a vacuum.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Adler cutting the phrase out of the air as the words are struck through on screen.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the loftier-problems objection by dissolving the individual in a vacuum.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike makes the rejection visible without sound — even a solitary worry contains other people.
storyboard.staging: Adler sweeps the phrase aside: no worry stands alone.

storyboard.claim: Even in sickness or facing death, other people's shadows are present — how will my family survive without me?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A family icon beside a photograph the young man holds with both hands.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Supplies the first people who remain inside a supposedly private fear.
storyboard.addedInformation: The photograph makes the others concrete: faces that outlive the questioner.
storyboard.staging: The young man looks down at the family photo: even dying is done among them.

storyboard.claim: The questions that haunt death are social: who remembers me, will I be a burden, did I contribute?
storyboard.concreteVisual: A grave marker — the death itself — standing in front of the man asking who will remember it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Extends the family question to the whole community and to legacy.
storyboard.addedInformation: The grave grounds the abstraction in the one fact all these questions assume: he dies.
storyboard.staging: The young man stands at a grave, asking the questions out loud.

storyboard.claim: Even the language you use to process your own death was given to you by a society — existence cannot be untangled from human connection.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The two men facing each other mid-sentence, passing the shared language between them — no single icon reads as a web of connection.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the objection: even the tools of solitary thought are borrowed from others.
storyboard.addedInformation: Turns the void sequence back into a two-person dialogue — connection is the frame after all.
storyboard.staging: The philosopher and the young man face each other, still arguing: the language itself is shared.
